Lesson 5 · Public synthetic edition

Uncertainty and conditional comparisons

Build intervals for the right target, reconstruct coefficient changes, and interpret interactions without losing the comparison.

Synthetic, reproducible examples. All case data in this lesson are newly generated from documented assumptions and fixed seeds. No historical source records or their fitted results are reused.

Stop 01 / 24

Name the uncertainty you are quantifying

A coefficient can vary because a new sample would contain different rows. A prediction can miss because a future outcome has fresh noise. A model can fail because the sample or specification does not represent the deployment setting. A confidence interval generally addresses the first source under stated assumptions; it does not absorb the other sources automatically.

We begin with an independent, correctly specified Gaussian experiment to derive classical intervals. We then move to Cedar, a fictional calibration-rig dataset with heteroskedastic errors, categories and interactions. Keeping these cases separate prevents a convenient formula from silently acquiring assumptions that the main example does not satisfy.

Pause and explain

Does a narrow confidence interval establish transportability to a different process?

Compare your reasoning
No. It may estimate a parameter precisely within the sampled population while saying little about a shifted population, a changed measurement process or an omitted mechanism.

Stop 02 / 24

An interval is a repeated-sampling procedure

X ∼ Uniform(0,10); Y = 12 + 2X + 4Z; Z ∼ N(0,1).

The independent interval example contains 80 rows. Holding the X design fixed, the lab generates 400 new outcome samples and calculates a two-sided 95% t interval for the slope each time. The fraction covering the known slope 2 is 94.75%. This finite simulation need not equal 95% exactly. Coverage refers to the long-run behavior of the procedure, not a probability assigned to a fixed frequentist parameter after seeing one interval.

Pause and explain

If an observed interval misses 2, was its 95% label necessarily false?

Compare your reasoning
No. A calibrated 95% procedure misses in roughly 5% of repeated samples. Calibration is a property of the procedure under its assumptions, not a guarantee for each realized interval.

Stop 03 / 24

Derive a slope interval with its assumptions

b = (XᵀX)⁻¹XᵀY; s² = SSE/(n−p).
Estimated Var(b) = s²(XᵀX)⁻¹.
CIⱼ = bⱼ ± t₁₋α/₂,n₋p × SE(bⱼ).

For the independent Gaussian example, the fitted intercept is 12.523, slope 1.909, and residual SD 3.930. There are 78 residual degrees of freedom. Independent normal homoskedastic errors and a correctly specified conditional mean make the t reference exact conditional on the design. Without normality, a large-sample approximation may still be useful, but its justification changes.

The same coefficient under three confidence levels
Nominal confidenceLower slope endpointUpper slope endpoint
90%1.6392.179
95%1.5862.232
99%1.4812.338

Pause and explain

Why does the interval widen as confidence increases?

Compare your reasoning
The estimate and standard error remain fixed; the critical value grows. More coverage requires a wider acceptance range for repeated-sample variation.

Stop 04 / 24

Change uncertainty without changing the fit

HC3 = (XᵀX)⁻¹ [Σ xᵢxᵢᵀ eᵢ²/(1−hᵢ)²] (XᵀX)⁻¹.

HC3 uses each squared residual with a leverage adjustment instead of one common error variance. It leaves the OLS coefficients and fitted values unchanged. It can support asymptotic inference for independent observations under heteroskedasticity and suitable regularity conditions; it does not repair a wrong target, omitted confounding, selection, dependence or a badly chosen mean model.

Cedar’s error SD grows with rig service age. Its main model therefore reports both conventional and HC3 standard errors. The classical covariance is retained as a comparison, not endorsed as calibrated. Clustered or serially dependent observations would need a different covariance design.

Pause and explain

Does “robust” mean the regression is resistant to all influential observations?

Compare your reasoning
No. HC3 is a heteroskedasticity-consistent covariance estimator with leverage adjustment. It is not robust regression, a cure for contamination or a license to ignore extreme design points.

Stop 05 / 24

Test a contrast rather than overlap

Var(bₐ−bᵦ) = Var(bₐ)+Var(bᵦ)−2Cov(bₐ,bᵦ).
For cᵀb: SE = √(cᵀ V c).

Two individual confidence intervals cannot generally determine whether their difference is statistically distinguishable from zero. The covariance term matters. Contrasts within one regression share fitted data and often have substantial covariance. Comparing separate group intervals is not a substitute for calculating the group difference directly.

A two-sided test and an interval agree when they use the same estimand, covariance, critical value and significance level: zero is outside the corresponding interval exactly when the test rejects. For nonlinear transformations, transform both endpoints when the transformation is monotone, and report the target scale.

Pause and explain

Can overlapping 95% intervals accompany a statistically significant difference?

Compare your reasoning
Yes. The standard error of the difference can be sufficiently small, especially with positive covariance. Compute the contrast and its covariance explicitly.

Stop 06 / 24

A mean and an individual need different intervals

At predictor vector x₀: ŷ₀ = x₀ᵀb.
SE(mean)² = x₀ᵀ V x₀.
SE(new outcome)² = x₀ᵀ V x₀ + s² under the classical model.

The mean interval describes uncertainty about the conditional expectation. The prediction interval adds the variation of a new independent outcome around that expectation. Even an enormous training sample cannot eliminate irreducible individual noise. These formulas concern a new row with known predictors, not a new estimate of a noisy or uncertain predictor.

Classical intervals in the separate Gaussian experiment

522.07021.193 to 22.94714.197 to 29.943
1031.61629.724 to 33.50923.567 to 39.666

Pause and explain

Why does the prediction interval not shrink to zero as sample size grows?

Compare your reasoning
Parameter uncertainty can shrink, but the future error remains. Conditional outcome variation is not eliminated by knowing the population mean exactly.

Stop 07 / 24

Locate where the design is informative

Simple regression: Var(ŷ₀ | X) = σ²[1/n + (x₀−x̄)² / Σ(xᵢ−x̄)²].

Mean uncertainty is smallest at the design center and grows away from it. A broad X range improves precision for a slope, while a large sample clustered at nearly one X value may still identify that slope poorly. The lab includes X = 12 to illustrate extrapolation beyond the generating interval. Its formula can be evaluated there, but the functional-form assumption does much more of the work.

Two uncertainty budgets over the predictor range — chart data

Pause and explain

Does a software interval at an unsupported X validate extrapolation?

Compare your reasoning
No. It quantifies uncertainty under the assumed model. Model misspecification outside observed support is not automatically reflected in the formula.

Stop 08 / 24

Work one prediction from the covariance

At X = 5, the separate Gaussian fit predicts 22.070. The estimated mean standard error is 0.441; adding the residual variance produces a new-outcome standard error of 3.955. The resulting 95% mean interval is 21.193 to 22.947, compared with 14.197 to 29.943 for a future outcome.

For a heteroskedastic model, adding one global s² to an HC3 mean variance does not create a justified individual prediction interval. You need a model or method for conditional outcome variation, such as a correctly specified distributional model, calibrated quantile method or an appropriately designed predictive calibration procedure.

If a model is fitted to log outcomes, a log-scale mean interval is not automatically an arithmetic-mean interval after exponentiation. That target requires retransformation and potentially uncertainty in the correction factor.

Pause and explain

What extra quantity separates the two classical intervals?

Compare your reasoning
The conditional variance of a new error. Parameter uncertainty appears in both; fresh outcome noise appears only in the prediction interval.

Stop 09 / 24

Introduce Cedar without inheriting the previous model

Cedar contains 260 simulated calibration rigs. Y is throughput in units/hour; E is service age in years; D marks a powered fixture; A is a tool setting between zero and one; bench category is amber, blue or copper. The generator uses seed 550829 and all features are available before calibration.

E ∼ Uniform(0,12); P(D=1|E) = logistic(−1+0.2E); Ec = E−6.
Y = 70 + 2Ec − 0.08Ec² + 5D + 1.1D Ec + 4A + 0.7EcA + bench offset + (3+0.4E)Z.

A is independent Uniform(0,1), Z is independent standard normal, and bench probabilities are 0.40, 0.35 and 0.25 with offsets 0, 4 and −3. Older rigs are more likely to have powered fixtures. This association makes the unconditional fixture contrast different from a comparison at a common service age.

Pause and explain

Why explicitly change the data passport between examples?

Compare your reasoning
Units, sampling, error structure and estimands changed. Carrying a previous case’s assumptions forward without restating them would make the inference misleading.

Stop 10 / 24

Read an adjusted coefficient as a conditional comparison

Additive approximation: Ŷ = b₀ + bD D + bE(E−6).

In the same-row additive model, the fixture coefficient is 2.489 units/hour. It compares the two fitted fixture groups at a common service age while imposing parallel service-age slopes. The unadjusted difference is 10.449. Adding a variable changes the comparison being made; it does not automatically reveal a “true effect.”

Unadjusted group means — chart data
GroupThroughput units/hour
No fixture68.8388
Powered fixture79.2877

The known generator has fixture-by-age interaction and curvature, so this additive fit is deliberately incomplete. Its coefficient is a linear projection coefficient, not the constant conditional fixture contrast of the full generator.

Pause and explain

What does “holding service age constant” mean algebraically?

Compare your reasoning
Compare two fitted values with the same service-age input and different D. It does not mean the data physically held each rig fixed or randomly assigned its fixture.

Stop 11 / 24

Hold the sample fixed when models change

Every Cedar coefficient comparison uses the same 260 rows. That is crucial: a coefficient can move because controls changed, because rows changed, or both. If a newly added covariate has missing values, first refit the shorter model on the common complete-case sample before attributing the difference to adjustment.

Composition differs across fixture groups
Fixture groupMean service yearsMean throughput
No fixture4.37268.839
Powered fixture6.90479.288

A complete-case sample can itself be selected. A defensible workflow records eligibility, missingness, measurement units and duplicate handling before interpreting adjusted coefficients. Here no outcome-based filtering or missing-data deletion occurs.

Pause and explain

Can the exact omitted-variable identity survive using different rows in the short and long models?

Compare your reasoning
Not in its usual same-sample form. Its algebra assumes identical outcomes, rows and weights, plus the stated nested regressors.

Stop 12 / 24

Precision depends on what controls leave

Residualize D on controls Z: rD = D − Z(ZᵀZ)⁻¹ZᵀD.
Homoskedastic Var(bD | X) = σ² / (rDᵀrD).

Before controlling for age, the centered fixture sum of squares is 64.688. After removing its linear association with centered age, the residual sum of squares is 55.586. The second quantity supplies the independent design variation that identifies the additive fixture coefficient. More controls can lower unexplained outcome noise while also consuming the variation used to estimate a particular coefficient.

Exact dependence prevents separate identification. Near dependence inflates uncertainty and can make coefficient values unstable even when combined predictions remain reasonably stable. The displayed homoskedastic variance formula is conceptual; Cedar’s reported uncertainty uses HC3 because its error spread changes with E.

Pause and explain

Does a high overall R² imply every individual coefficient is precise?

Compare your reasoning
No. Predictors may jointly explain Y while being highly correlated with each other. Precision for one coefficient depends on its residual variation after the others are removed.

Stop 13 / 24

Reproduce the coefficient by residualizing

Frisch–Waugh–Lovell: bD = (rDᵀrY)/(rDᵀrD),
where rY and rD both remove the same control columns, including the intercept.

The lab regresses D on intercept and centered service age, then does the same for Y. Regressing the resulting Y residuals on the D residuals gives 2.48925816, exactly the additive fixture coefficient 2.48925816 up to rounding. This is a computational identity, not a new identification assumption.

Residualizing only Y, changing rows between the steps or omitting an intercept from just one projection breaks the intended comparison. The two-step coefficient identity does not mean that a naive second-stage standard error automatically has the correct degrees of freedom or covariance treatment.

Pause and explain

Why residualize the treatment indicator as well as the outcome?

Compare your reasoning
The coefficient must use the part of D not already explained by the controls. Residualizing only Y leaves the denominator’s irrelevant variation in place.

Stop 14 / 24

Account for the coefficient movement exactly

Short Y on (1,D): bDshort.
Long Y on (1,D,Ec): bDlong, bElong.
Auxiliary Ec on (1,D): δD.
bDshort = bDlong + bElong δD.

The long fixture coefficient is 2.489258, the long age coefficient 3.144374, and the auxiliary fixture slope 2.531407. Their product is 7.959688. Adding it to the long fixture coefficient reconstructs 10.448946, the short coefficient. The observed shift is 7.959688. The script asserts equality numerically.

The sign can be reasoned through before multiplying: fixture status is associated with greater service age, and age has a positive additive partial slope in this sample. Their product raises the unadjusted fixture coefficient.

Pause and explain

Does this identity require the long regression to be the true population model?

Compare your reasoning
No. It is exact same-sample least-squares algebra. Calling the difference causal omitted-variable bias requires additional assumptions about the population model and the target effect.

Stop 15 / 24

Do not rename every difference “bias”

The OVB identity explains why coefficients differ between two linear projections. To call the short coefficient biased for a causal effect, specify a structural target and show why the long model identifies it. A control can be a confounder, mediator, collider or proxy; adding it can improve or worsen causal interpretation depending on the data-generating process.

Cedar’s full DGP is disclosed for teaching. In an empirical application it would not be known. A distributional imbalance is a clue to investigate, not proof of a causal pathway. Even in Cedar, the fixture contrast varies with service age, so a single additive fixture coefficient is not the entire response surface.

  • Name the estimand before diagnosing bias.
  • Draw the measurement and assignment story.
  • Check overlap for the intended contrast.
  • Distinguish sampling algebra from causal assumptions.

Pause and explain

If a coefficient barely changes after adding one control, is confounding ruled out?

Compare your reasoning
No. Unobserved confounding can remain, the control may be weakly measured, or offsetting omitted pathways may hide movement.

Stop 16 / 24

Interpret curvature through a derivative or contrast

Full-model age slope = bE + 2bE² Ec + bD×E D + bE×A A.

For powered fixtures at tool setting A = 0.5, the fitted local service-age slopes at E = 3, 6 and 9 are 4.097, 3.367, 2.638 throughput units/hour per service year. Each is a combination of several coefficients. A coefficient labelled “service age” alone refers to the centered reference point and specified interacting predictors.

For a finite change, construct two complete design rows and subtract their fitted values. A derivative is local, while a multi-year contrast follows the whole fitted curve. A quadratic turning point is a property of a fitted equation; it is not a maintenance or retirement recommendation by itself.

Pause and explain

Can you read the age-squared coefficient as the effect of adding one year?

Compare your reasoning
No. It contributes to the changing slope together with the linear and interaction terms. Use a derivative at stated inputs or an explicit finite contrast.

Stop 17 / 24

Test several restrictions as one hypothesis

Classical nested F = [(SSER − SSEU)/q] / [SSEU/(n−pU)].
Robust Wald W = (Rb)ᵀ[R VHC3 Rᵀ]⁻¹(Rb), compared asymptotically with χ²q.

Here the joint null sets age curvature and fixture-by-age interaction to zero: q = 2. The restricted SSE is 8,280.044 and unrestricted SSE 7,686.186 with 251 residual degrees of freedom. The classical F statistic is 9.697 (p = 0.0000878), but its exact homoskedastic calibration is not valid for this generator. The HC3 Wald statistic is 22.856 (asymptotic p = 0.0000109).

Two separate marginal tests do not answer the same joint question. Their covariance matters, and a pair of individually noisy coefficients can be jointly informative. Statistical rejection still does not establish decision importance.

Pause and explain

Why report the classical F only as a comparison here?

Compare your reasoning
Cedar’s conditional error variance changes with service age. The displayed exact F distribution relies on assumptions that the main DGP intentionally violates.

Stop 18 / 24

Treat category labels as labels

Amber, blue and copper are bench types, not equally spaced numbers. With an intercept, use two indicators and an omitted reference category. Including all three indicators creates exact dependence because they sum to the intercept. Changing the reference alters coefficient labels but leaves the fitted comparison surface unchanged.

Category sample composition

Amber10073.894
Blue8278.428
Copper7870.897

With amber as reference, the centered full-model intercept is 70.774. With copper as reference it is 68.400. The maximum absolute fitted-value difference after reparameterization is 0.0000000000. This numerical equality is checked in the lab. The raw category means above are not the adjusted indicator coefficients.

Pause and explain

Why not assign amber = 1, blue = 2 and copper = 3 as one numeric predictor?

Compare your reasoning
That imposes an ordering and equal spacing on the fitted effects. Such a restriction requires substantive justification, not just a convenient code.

Stop 19 / 24

Let the fixture comparison vary with age

Fixture contrast at age E = bD + bD×E(E−6).

Centering age at six makes the main fixture coefficient answer a meaningful reference-point question. The interaction coefficient says how the fixture contrast changes per additional service year. Neither coefficient alone describes the contrast at every age. HC3 uncertainty for each contrast uses the full covariance, including the covariance between main and interaction terms.

Pause and explain

What happens to fitted values if age is centered somewhere else?

Compare your reasoning
They remain the same when all lower-order and interaction terms are transformed consistently. Main-effect coefficients change their reference point, not the underlying fitted surface.

Stop 20 / 24

Read a continuous interaction as a surface

Tool-setting slope at service age E = bA + bE×A(E−6).

At E = 3, 6 and 9, the fitted tool-setting slopes are 1.682, 5.102, 8.522 throughput units/hour per full unit of A. For a smaller setting change multiply by that change while holding age fixed. A full-unit difference spans the entire generated tool-setting range, so it should not be treated as a typical local adjustment.

An interaction describes dependence of one fitted slope on another predictor. Preserve the associated lower-order terms unless a well-justified restriction says otherwise. Explain the surface with a small number of supported contrasts, rather than listing coefficients without their reference points.

Pause and explain

Does a positive interaction guarantee that increasing either predictor always increases the outcome?

Compare your reasoning
No. Each local slope combines its main effect and the interaction evaluated at the other predictor. The sign can vary across the supported range.

The printed coefficient count is meaningful only if the design is full rank; the script uses an identifiable basis. Conventional and HC3 standard errors can differ in either direction. “Robust” does not mean “always larger.”

The full model contains known mean terms from the teaching DGP. That makes it useful for demonstrating covariance calculations, but real modeling rarely enjoys this certainty. Interpretation still depends on measurement, common support, target population and the purpose of adjustment.

Pause and explain

Should you select the covariance estimator that makes the preferred coefficient significant?

Compare your reasoning
No. Choose the uncertainty method to match sampling and dependence assumptions, not the desired p-value.

Stop 22 / 24

Read observed-versus-predicted axes carefully

The horizontal axis below is observed throughput and the vertical axis is cross-fitted predicted throughput. A point above the diagonal has predicted greater than observed, so its residual Y − Ŷ is negative. A point below the diagonal is underpredicted and has a positive residual. Reversing the axes reverses the visual rule but not the residual definition.

For repeated measurements from one rig or one facility, split by that grouping if the intended task is a new rig or facility. Random row folds can otherwise leak stable identity or environment information.

Pause and explain

Why use cross-fitted rather than training residuals for a performance shortlist?

Compare your reasoning
Training predictions have already adapted to each row’s outcome. Cross-fitting reduces that self-fit advantage, although it does not eliminate selection effects or guarantee a fair interpretation.

Stop 24 / 24

Deliver a conditional, testable claim

A careful Cedar handoff separates four statements: the unadjusted fixture difference is 10.449 units/hour; the additive age-adjusted coefficient is 2.489; the full model permits age-varying contrasts; and robust uncertainty addresses heteroskedasticity under independent sampling. The exact additive coefficient change is verified by the auxiliary regression, not explained causally by algebra alone.

  • For a coefficient: name the contrast, reference point and covariance method.
  • For an average: use uncertainty in the conditional mean.
  • For a new outcome: add the appropriate conditional outcome variation.
  • For action: investigate design, measurement and consequences beyond the fitted residual.

The notebook reproduces all estimates, interval endpoints, covariance calculations, tests and residual rankings. Its assertions verify FWL, the omitted-variable identity and reference-category invariance. Next, Lesson 6 turns the emphasis from explaining a fitted sample to forecasting genuinely new cases.

Pause and explain

What is the strongest unsupported leap to avoid?

Compare your reasoning
Do not turn an adjusted association or a residual into a causal conclusion or an individual operational judgment without the additional evidence that decision requires.

All case observations are generated for teaching. They are not evidence about real people, firms or markets. Provenance and reproduction
